title: Google Ads vs Meta Ads: Where Should an E-commerce Brand Spend First?
metaTitle: Google Ads vs Meta Ads for E-commerce: Where to Start
metaDescription: Google captures demand that already exists; Meta creates it. How to choose your first ad platform, split a budget, and judge results honestly.
excerpt: Google Ads reaches people already searching for what you sell. Meta Ads puts your product in front of people who were not looking. Which one deserves your first budget depends on your product, your margins and how much creative you can produce.

faqs.q: Is Google Ads or Meta Ads better for e-commerce?
faqs.a: Neither is better in general. Google Ads suits products people already search for by name or category, because it captures existing demand. Meta Ads suits products people discover visually and buy on impulse, because it creates demand. Most established e-commerce brands end up using both, with Google capturing demand that Meta helps create.

faqs.q: How much budget do I need to test an ad platform?
faqs.a: Enough to produce a meaningful number of purchases, not just clicks. A practical rule is to budget for at least a few dozen conversions per campaign over the test period, so the platform's bidding has data to learn from and you can tell signal from noise. For a low-priced product that can be a modest budget; for a high-priced one it is considerably more.

faqs.q: How long should I run ads before judging the results?
faqs.a: Give a new campaign two to four weeks before drawing conclusions, and avoid large changes in the first week while the platform is still learning. Judge it over at least one full buying cycle for your product, and compare against your break-even return on ad spend rather than against a generic benchmark.

faqs.q: Should I run Google and Meta ads at the same time?
faqs.a: Yes, once one platform is profitable. They do different jobs: Meta introduces people to the brand, and many of them later search for it on Google. Running both also protects you from depending on a single platform. Start with one, get it working, then add the second with its own budget and its own targets.

body:
Every e-commerce founder with a first advertising budget asks the same question: Google or Meta? The honest answer is that they do different jobs, and the right first choice depends on what you sell. This guide explains the difference, shows how to choose, and covers how to judge the results without fooling yourself.

## The core difference: capturing demand vs creating it

**Google Ads captures demand that already exists.** Someone types "men's oud perfume" or "standing desk Dubai" and sees your product. They were already looking. Your ad competes on relevance and price at the moment of intent.

**Meta Ads creates demand.** Someone is scrolling Instagram or Facebook, not looking for anything, and your ad interrupts with a product they had not thought about. Your ad competes on attention.

That one difference drives almost everything else: what the ads cost, what creative you need, and how quickly sales arrive.

## When Google Ads should come first

Start with Google when people already search for what you sell.

- Your product belongs to a known category with real search volume.
- Buyers compare options and prices before purchasing.
- The purchase solves a specific need: a replacement part, a gift, a refill.
- You have a product feed in good shape, so Shopping and Performance Max campaigns can show your products with images and prices.

Google's strength is intent. The weakness is that demand is finite: you can only reach as many people as are searching, and popular terms are expensive because every competitor wants them.

## When Meta Ads should come first

Start with Meta when the product sells on sight.

- It is visual, new or hard to describe in a search term.
- People buy it on impulse, or as a treat, rather than researching it.
- It solves a problem people did not know had a product.
- You can produce a steady supply of video and image creative.

Meta's strength is scale: you can reach almost anyone. The weakness is that it lives or dies on creative. The same budget behind a weak video and a strong one can produce wildly different results, and creative wears out as people see it repeatedly. That is why brands that do well on Meta treat [ad creatives](/media/ad-creatives/) and [UGC ads](/media/ugc-ads/) as an ongoing production line, not a one-off task.

## What each platform needs from you

**For Google**, the work is mostly structure and data: an accurate product feed, sensible campaign structure, negative keywords so you do not pay for irrelevant searches, and landing pages that match what the ad promised.

**For Meta**, the work is mostly creative and testing: several different concepts, each in a few variations, a clear offer, and a product page that loads fast on a phone.

**For both**, tracking has to be right before you spend. That means conversion tracking that records real purchases and their value, and server-side tracking where possible, because browser-only tracking misses a share of sales. Without it, the platforms optimise toward the wrong thing and your reports mislead you.

## How to split a budget

There is no universal split, but these starting points are reasonable.

- **A product people search for:** put most of the first budget into Google, with a smaller Meta budget for retargeting visitors who did not buy.
- **A visual, impulse product:** put most into Meta, with a small Google budget covering searches for your own brand name.
- **An established store with both working:** fund each platform according to what it returns at the margin, and move budget gradually rather than in big swings.

Whatever the split, keep a small share for testing new creative or new audiences. An account that only runs what already works slowly stops working.

## How to judge the results

This is where most advertisers go wrong. The return on ad spend (ROAS) shown inside each platform is not the truth, because both platforms claim credit for the same sale. A customer who saw a Meta ad and later clicked a Google ad is counted by both.

Three habits keep you honest:

- Know your break-even ROAS before you start. It depends on your margin, not on an industry benchmark.
- Look at blended results: total revenue divided by total ad spend across all platforms.
- Compare new-customer revenue separately from returning-customer revenue, because retargeting existing customers always looks good.

We cover this in detail in [our guide to measuring ROAS properly](/blog/measuring-roas-properly/).

## Common mistakes

- **Judging too early.** Changing budgets and audiences every two days never lets a campaign finish learning.
- **Spreading a small budget across too many campaigns.** Each one ends up with too little data to optimise.
- **Sending ads to a slow or confusing page.** The ad did its job; the page lost the sale. Often the cheapest improvement is to the store itself.
- **Ignoring search engine optimization.** Ads stop the moment you stop paying. [SEO](/marketing/seo/) builds traffic that keeps arriving, and lowers how much you need to spend on ads over time.
- **Running the same creative for months.** Performance falls as the audience tires of it.

## A simple way to decide

Ask two questions. Do people already search for this kind of product? Can I produce new creative every month?

If the first answer is yes, begin with Google. If the first is no and the second is yes, begin with Meta. If both are yes, begin with whichever you can execute best, get it profitable, then add the other.
